title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 18, 1773/74, pp. 85ff; this is p. 93). Euler fixes a prime P and a base a, and studies the 'series of residues' 1, a, a^2, ... mod P. In modern terms this is the cyclic subgroup <a> of (Z/PZ)^*. Earlier sections showed three things: this series is closed under multiplication (§24), it is closed under division (§25), and its length divides P-1.

§26 (completed on this page): since 1 lies in the series, every residue mu has an omega in the series with mu*omega ≡ 1 (mod P). Euler calls such a pair 'socia', i.e. mutual inverses. Hence the terms of any residue series can be arranged in inverse pairs. The only exceptions are 1, which is its own socius, and -1 if it occurs, which is also its own socius.

§27 is a programmatic remark. These preliminaries were treated 'more fully elsewhere' (most likely E262 of 1761). Euler now proceeds to theorems proved 'from quite singular principles', for which the usual methods are too hard. The goal is his attempt to prove that primitive roots exist.

§28 Theorem: the congruence x^n ≡ 1 (mod P) has at most n solutions with 0 < x < P. The proof is begun by cases:
- n = 1: only x = 1.
- n = 2: P divides (x-1)(x+1), so x = 1 or x = P-1.
- n = 3: begun here and finished on p. 94. (x-1)(x^2+x+1); if a is a root of the quadratic factor, so is a^2. A third root b would force P | (a-b)(a+b+1), giving b = a or b ≡ a^2.

The general case (p. 94) uses the factor theorem mod P: divide by x - a, getting a form of lower degree, and induct, 'as in the resolution of equations'. If a is a root, then 1, a, ..., a^{n-1} are roots. This is the lemma later fed into Euler's primitive-root argument.
errors: Implicit gap on this page: the claim that residues pair off with only 1 and -1 self-associated needs x^2 ≡ 1 ⇒ x ≡ ±1. That fact is proved only just below (case n = 2 of §28), not before §26. The statement is correct, but the order of proof is slightly inverted.
Not an error on this page, but relevant: the larger argument that §28 serves (existence of primitive roots, later in E449) was judged incomplete by Gauss, Disquisitiones art. 56.
The case analysis for n = 2 and n = 3 assumes P prime (P divides a product, so it divides a factor). This is correctly invoked.

ideas.what: Every element of the cyclic residue series a^k mod P has an inverse in the same series. Elements pair off as mutual inverses ('socia'), with 1 and -1 self-paired.
ideas.modern_name: Closure of a subgroup under inverses; inverse pairing in (Z/pZ)^* (the device behind the pairing proof of Wilson's theorem)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Inverses mod p: Euler (E262, 1761). Pairing proof of Wilson's theorem usually associated with Gauss (Disq. Arith. art. 77, 1801), with earlier hints by Euler/Lagrange.
ideas.where_published: E262 (Novi Comm. 7, 1761) treats residue series; this page (E449). The terminology 'socia' is also used in Euler's later Wilson-theorem work (E560, Opuscula analytica I, 1783), as far as I recall (unsure of exact wording).

ideas.what: x^n ≡ 1 (mod P) has at most n solutions below P. Proved by explicit cases n = 1, 2, 3 and then via the factor theorem mod P.
ideas.modern_name: A polynomial of degree n over the field F_p has at most n roots (Lagrange's theorem on polynomial congruences)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1768/1770, Nouv. Mém. Acad. Berlin); used informally by Euler earlier
ideas.where_published: E449 (this paper); related informal use in E262 and in Euler's 1750s work on Fermat's theorem.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains standard, well-documented material from a famous paper: inverses mod p, and the bound of at most n roots for x^n - 1 mod p. Both are known in the literature, and E449 is explicitly discussed by Gauss. Nothing new.

In the theorem the image shows 'x < P' with a mark under the sign (possibly a damaged '<'). The meaning is 0 < x < P.
